title: Zariski's Main localization at a quasi-finite prime
statement: Let $A\to B$ be a ring map of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], let $B'\subseteq B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $B$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], and let $\mathfrak q\subseteq B$ be a prime ideal at which $A\to B$ is quasi-finite [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] (Stacks Algebra Definition 00PL). Then there is an element $h\in B'$ with $h\notin\mathfrak q$ such that the map $B'_h\to B_h$, $y/h^n\mapsto y/h^n$, between the localizations at the powers of $h$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] induced by the inclusion $B'\subseteq B$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779) and its proof (lines 30788-30877); used in literature/stacks-project/more-algebra.tex:2524-2529 (proof of Lemma Tag 09XH)

proof.text: *Notation and the inductive claim.* Write $R=A$, $S=B$, $S'=B'$. For a ring map $R\to T$ and $t_1,\dots,t_n\in T$ write $R[t_1,\dots,t_n]\subseteq T$ for the $R$-subalgebra generated by the $t_i$ (the image of $R[X_1,\dots,X_n]$, $X_i\mapsto t_i$). For $n\ge0$ let $P(n)$ be the claim: *for every ring map $R\to S$ of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], every prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ at which $R\to S$ is quasi-finite [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] and all $x_1,\dots,x_n\in S$ such that $S$ is a finitely generated $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], there is $g$ in the integral closure $S'$ of $R$ in $S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] with $g\notin\mathfrak q$ such that $S'_g\to S_g$, $y/g^k\mapsto y/g^k$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], is an isomorphism.* If $x_1,\dots,x_n$ generate $S$ as an $R$-algebra then $S=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is generated as a module over itself by $1$, so $P(n)$ for this $n$ is the statement. We prove $P(n)$ for all $n$ by induction: $P(0)$ (step 4), $P(1)$ (steps 5-10), and $P(n)$ for $n\ge2$ from $P(1)$ and $P(n-1)$ (steps 11-15). (The source inducts on the minimal such $n$; this is the same induction.)

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), first paragraph

proof.text: *An integral closure is integrally closed.* Let $C\to T$ be a ring map and $D\subseteq T$ the integral closure of $C$ in $T$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. If $t\in T$ is integral over $D$, then $t\in D$. Indeed $D[t]$ is generated as a $D$-algebra by one element integral over $D$, so it is a finitely generated $D$-module by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-of-integral-generators], hence integral over $D$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]; $D$ is integral over $C$, so $D[t]$ is integral over $C$ by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive]; thus $t$ is integral over $C$, i.e. $t\in D$. In particular the integral closure of $D$ in $T$ is $D$ itself, and $D$ is integrally closed in $T$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 1: 'in other words R = S''; Algebra Lemma Tag 00GN (lemma-integral-transitive)

proof.text: *Localization bookkeeping* [def-weil-ring-localization-away], used below. (i) If $C\subseteq T$ is a subring and $c\in C$, then $C_c\to T_c$ is injective: if $y/c^k\mapsto0$ then $c^my=0$ in $T$ for some $m$, hence in $C$, so $y/c^k=0$ in $C_c$. (ii) If $\alpha:C\to T$ is a ring map, $c,d\in C$ and $C_c\to T_{\alpha(c)}$ is an isomorphism, then so is $C_{cd}\to T_{\alpha(cd)}$, being its localization at $d/1$. (iii) If $c,d,e\in T$ satisfy $c^m(c^kd-e)=0$ for some $m,k\ge0$, then a ring map out of $T$ inverts $c$ and $d$ if and only if it inverts $c$ and $e$ (after inverting $c$, $e=c^kd$); hence $T_{cd}$ and $T_{ce}$ are the same localization of $T$, compatibly with any map out of $T$.

proof.text: *Case $n=0$.* Here $S$ is a finitely generated module over the image of $R$, so every element of $S$ is integral over $R$ by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]; hence $S'=S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], and $g=1\notin\mathfrak q$ works, $S'_1\to S_1$ being the identity.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 0 (Lemma Tag 00GK)

proof.text: *Case $n=1$: reduction to $R$ integrally closed in $S$.* Let $R\to S$, $\mathfrak q$, $x=x_1$ be as in $P(1)$. The generators of $S$ as an $R$-algebra generate it as an $S'$-algebra, so $S'\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]; module generators of $S$ over $R[x]$ generate $S$ over $S'[x]\supseteq R[x]$; by [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-prime-permanence] (with $A\to B\to C$ equal to $R\to S'\to S$) the map $S'\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]; and by step 2 $S'$ is integrally closed in $S$. The conclusion of $P(1)$ concerns only $S'\subseteq S$. So it suffices to prove: $(*)$ *if $R\subseteq S$ is a subring integrally closed in $S$, $R\to S$ is of finite type and quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$, and $S$ is a finitely generated $R[x]$-module for some $x\in S$, then there is $h\in R$, $h\notin\mathfrak q$, with $R_h\to S_h$ an isomorphism*; applied to $S'\subseteq S$ it gives $P(1)$ with $g=h$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 1, first sentences (Lemma Tag 0C6H)

proof.text: *Case $n=1$: the conductor.* In the situation of $(*)$ let $\varphi:R[X]\to S$ be the $R$-algebra map with $X\mapsto x$ [def-weil-polynomial-ring]; $\varphi(R[X])=R[x]$ and $S$ is a finitely generated $R[X]$-module via $\varphi$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Let $J=\{g\in S\mid gS\subseteq\varphi(R[X])\}$ and $\sqrt J$ its radical. Since $R$ is integrally closed in $S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], [lem-weil-pbc-conductor-radical-coefficients] applies: $u\varphi(\sum a_iX^i)\in\sqrt J$ with $u\in S$, $a_i\in R$ implies $ua_i\in\sqrt J$ for all $i$. Put $\bar R=R/(R\cap\sqrt J)$ and $\bar S=S/\sqrt J$. The induced map $\bar R\to\bar S$ is injective, so $\bar R$ is a subring of $\bar S$; $\bar S$ is reduced ($s^m\in\sqrt J$ implies $s\in\sqrt J$), hence so is $\bar R$; $\bar S$ is a finitely generated $\bar R[\bar x]$-module (images of module generators). And $\bar x$ is strongly transcendental over $\bar R$ [def-weil-pbc-strongly-transcendental]: if $\bar u\sum\bar a_i\bar x^i=0$ in $\bar S$, lift to $u\in S$, $a_i\in R$; then $u\varphi(\sum a_iX^i)\in\sqrt J$, so $ua_i\in\sqrt J$, i.e. $\bar u\bar a_i=0$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 1, the diagram and 'According to Lemma 00PY' (Situation Tag 00PW, Lemma Tag 00PY)

proof.text: *Case $n=1$: $\mathfrak q\not\supseteq J$.* By [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-strongly-transcendental-not-quasi-finite] (applied to $\bar R\subseteq\bar S$ and $\bar x$, step 6) the map $\bar R\to\bar S$ is quasi-finite at no prime of $\bar S$. Suppose $J\subseteq\mathfrak q$; then $\sqrt J\subseteq\mathfrak q$ since $\mathfrak q$ is prime, and $\bar{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak q/\sqrt J$ is a prime of $\bar S$ whose inverse image in $S$ is $\mathfrak q$. The square $R\to S$, $R\to\bar R$, $\bar R\to\bar S$, $S\to\bar S$ commutes, $R\to S$ is of finite type, and $\bar S$ is the image of $S$, so [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-four-rings] applies with $\mathfrak q'=\bar{\mathfrak q}$: since $R\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime], $\bar R\to\bar S$ is quasi-finite at $\bar{\mathfrak q}$, a contradiction. Hence there is $s\in J$ with $s\notin\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 1, 'Hence by Lemma 00Q2 ... By Lemma 00PN we deduce that q does not lie in V(J)'

proof.text: *Case $n=1$: the monogenic subalgebra.* Let $C=\varphi(R[X])=R[x]\subseteq S$; $\varphi$ induces $R[X]/I\cong C$ with $I=\ker\varphi$, and $R\to C$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. Since $s\in J$, $s=s\cdot1\in C$, say $s=\varphi(f)$. The map $C_s\to S_s$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is injective by step 3(i) and surjective because $t/s^k=ts/s^{k+1}$ with $ts\in C$; so it is an isomorphism of $R$-algebras. Let $\mathfrak q_C=\mathfrak q\cap C$; $s\notin\mathfrak q_C$. By [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-prime-principal-localization] for $R\to S$ (with $f=1$, $g=s$) the map $R\to S_s$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak qS_s$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. The isomorphism $C_s\cong S_s$ of $R$-algebras pulls $\mathfrak qS_s$ back to $\mathfrak q_CC_s$ and induces an isomorphism of the fibre rings over the same prime of $R$ matching these primes, so $R\to C_s$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q_CC_s$; by the same lemma for $R\to C$ (with $f=1$, $g=s$) $R\to C$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q_C$. Finally an element of $C$ integral over $R$ is an element of $S$ integral over $R$, hence lies in $R$: the integral closure of $R$ in $C$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is $R$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n = 1, 'Let I = Ker(φ) ... see Lemma 077H. Note that R is integrally closed in R[x]/I'

proof.text: *Case $n=1$: Zariski's Main Theorem for $C\cong R[X]/I$.* By [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-monogenic-integral-closure] applied to $R$, $I$, $C\cong R[X]/I$ and $\mathfrak q_C$ (step 8: $R\to C$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q_C$ and the integral closure of $R$ in $C$ is $R$), there is $h\in R$ with $h\notin\mathfrak q_C$, i.e. $h\notin\mathfrak q$, such that $R_h\to C_h$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is an isomorphism.

proof.text: *Case $n\ge2$: the integral closure of $R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]$.* Assume $P(1)$ and $P(n-1)$, and let $R\to S$, $\mathfrak q$, $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be as in $P(n)$. Let $A_{n-1}=R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]\subseteq S$ and let $R'\subseteq S$ be the integral closure of $A_{n-1}$ in $S$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. Then $R'\to S$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], $S$ is a finitely generated $R'[x_n]$-module (since $R'[x_n]\supseteq R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$) [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], and $R'\to S$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ by [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-prime-permanence] applied to $R\to R'\to S$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. By $P(1)$ for $R'\to S$, $\mathfrak q$, $x_n$ there is $g'$ in the integral closure of $R'$ in $S$, which is $R'$ by step 2, with $g'\notin\mathfrak q$ and $R'_{g'}\to S_{g'}$ an isomorphism.

proof.text: *Case $n\ge2$: a finite subalgebra $R''$.* Let $s_1,\dots,s_m$ generate $S$ as an $R$-algebra. By surjectivity of $R'_{g'}\to S_{g'}$ choose $y_j\in R'$ and $k_j\ge0$ with $s_j/1=y_j/g'^{k_j}$ in $S_{g'}$. Let $R''=R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1},y_1,\dots,y_m,g']\subseteq R'$. The map $R''_{g'}\to S_{g'}$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is injective by step 3(i), and surjective since its image is an $R$-subalgebra containing $1/g'$ and all $s_j/1$, which generate $S_{g'}$ as an $R$-algebra (every element is $P(s_1,\dots,s_m)/g'^k$); so it is an isomorphism. $R''$ is generated as an $A_{n-1}$-algebra by $y_1,\dots,y_m,g'\in R'$, which are integral over $A_{n-1}$, so $R''$ is a finitely generated $A_{n-1}$-module by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-of-integral-generators] [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Hence $R\to R''$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\in R''$, and $R''$ is a finitely generated module over $R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]=A_{n-1}\subseteq R''$.

source.place: Algebra, proof of Theorem Tag 00Q9 (theorem-main-theorem, line 30779), case n > 1, construction of R'' (Lemma Tag 00GM)

proof.text: *Case $n\ge2$: $R\to R''$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q''=\mathfrak q\cap R''$.* Note $g'\notin\mathfrak q''$. By [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-at-prime-principal-localization] for $R\to S$ ($f=1$, $g=g'$), $R\to S_{g'}$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak qS_{g'}$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. The $R$-algebra isomorphism $R''_{g'}\cong S_{g'}$ of step 12 pulls $\mathfrak qS_{g'}$ back to $\mathfrak q''R''_{g'}$ and identifies the fibre rings over the same prime of $R$, so $R\to R''_{g'}$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q''R''_{g'}$; by the same lemma for $R\to R''$ ($f=1$, $g=g'$), $R\to R''$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q''$. (The source argues with $(R'')_{\mathfrak q''}=S_{\mathfrak q}$ and Lemma 00PK; the principal localization gives the same conclusion with Lemma 077H.)

proof.text: *Case $n\ge2$: conclusion.* $R'''_g\to R''_g$ is an isomorphism, the localization of $R'''_{g''}\to R''_{g''}$ at $g'''$ (step 3(ii)). By step 3(iii) (with the relation of step 14) $R''_g=R''_{g''g'}$ and $S_g=S_{g''g'}$, and $R''_{g''g'}\to S_{g''g'}$ is an isomorphism, the localization of $R''_{g'}\to S_{g'}$ (step 12) at $g''$. So the natural map $R'''_g\to S_g$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away] is an isomorphism. Every element of $R'''$ is an element of $S$ integral over $R$, so $R'''\subseteq S'$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], and $R'''_g\to S_g$ factors as $R'''_g\to S'_g\to S_g$. The second map is injective (step 3(i)) and surjective because the composite is; so $S'_g\to S_g$ is an isomorphism, with $g\in S'$, $g\notin\mathfrak q$. This proves $P(n)$ and completes the induction.
